turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: I'm afraid I don't know where Estella is, ma'am, but I can go look for her, if it would please you.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Estella will show you the way to play the game, which is the only thing that brings me any joy. Go and find her, and tell her to come to me at once.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: I'll go find Estella right away, ma'am, but if it's not too much trouble, could I ask if it's...if it's a game that's...gentle, ma'am?

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Do not waste time asking such questions, boy. You will play the game as I have instructed, and that is all.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: I'll go find Estella, ma'am, but I must confess, I'm not quite sure what to make of the game you've described. I'm afraid I'm not very good at games, and I don't want to cause any trouble.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: You will play the game, boy, and you will not question me. I have instructed Estella to teach you, and you will obey her as you would me.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: I beg your pardon, ma'am, but I'm afraid I'm not quite sure I can play a game that requires...attention from Estella. I'm not one for games that involve...competing, ma'am.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: You will play the game, boy, and you will do as I say, lest you disappoint Estella and shame yourself. I will not be disobeyed.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: I don't mean to be disobedient, ma'am, but I'm afraid I'm not comfortable with the idea of competing with Estella, and I worry it might be...unfair to her.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: You will do as I say, Pip, because it is my will, and you will not question the instructions of your betters. You will play the game, and you will not think of fairness or compassion, for those are weaknesses, and I will not have them in my household.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: I'm afraid I'm not sure I can, ma'am, for my sister, Maggie, and I, we rely on our sister, Mrs. Joe, for support, and I fear I'd be in the way here, and it wouldn't be fair to Estella or you, ma'am.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: You will not think of your sister, or your sister's husband, or your own meager circumstances, Pip. You will think only of Estella, and how you may impress her, and make her smile.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: I'm not sure I understand, ma'am, why I must play the game, and what it would accomplish, if it's only to make Estella smile?

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: You are a foolish child, Pip, to question my intentions and the value of Estella's smiles. I will tell you what it will accomplish: it will break your spirit, and make you more worthy of me, and of Estella's company.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: I-I don't think I want to play the game, ma'am, if it's only to break my spirit, for I value my spirit, and I fear it would be cruel to do so.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: You will learn to value nothing but Estella's smiles, Pip, and you will do so in the only way I deem worthy, which is through submission and obedience.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: But, ma'am, how can I learn to value Estella's smiles if I don't know what they mean, or if they're even genuine?

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: You will learn to read the value of Estella's smiles, Pip, as I have learned to read the value of my own sorrow and heartache, and it is a lesson that will serve you well in life.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: But, ma'am, I'm not sure I can even play the game, for I'm not used to such...such grand ways of doing things, and I fear I might make a mistake and bring shame upon myself and my family.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: You would do well to remember, Pip, that you are here to learn and to obey, not to question or to make excuses.

opening.speaker: Pip
opening.text: Mr. Pumblechook’s boy, ma’am. Come—to play.

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: Come nearer; let me look at you. Come close.

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: Look at me. You are not afraid of a woman who has never seen the sun since you were born?

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: Do you know what I touch here?

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: I am tired. I want diversion, and I have done with men and women. Play.

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: I sometimes have sick fancies, and I have a sick fancy that I want to see some play. There, there!

opening.speaker: Pip
opening.text: No, ma’am, I am very sorry for you, and very sorry I can’t play just now. If you complain of me I shall get into trouble with my sister, so I would do it if I could; but it’s so new here, and so strange, and so fine,—and melancholy—.
